strengths: Addresses a realistic and underexplored problem setting: leveraging reward-free, mixed-quality, multi-embodiment offline data for RL, which lifts several restrictive assumptions of prior offline-to-online RL work.

Unusually extensive empirical evaluation spanning 72 tasks across DMControl and Meta-World (locomotion and manipulation), roughly 12x more tasks than prior world-model pretraining papers, which strengthens the credibility of the claimed general applicability.

Clear empirical motivation for the proposed techniques via t-SNE/Wasserstein-distance analysis showing distributional shift between offline pretraining and online fine-tuning data, which grounds the design of experience rehearsal and execution guidance.

Comprehensive baseline comparisons, including representation-learning baselines (R3M), offline-data-reuse RL baselines (UDS, ExPLORe), JSRL-BC, imitation learning (Diffusion Policy), other world-model pretraining methods (iVideoGPT, pretrained DreamerV3), and a continual-learning baseline (PackNet).
Thorough ablation studies isolating the contribution of pretraining, experience rehearsal, and execution guidance, as well as which world model components benefit most from fine-tuning.

Reasonably transparent reporting of implementation difficulties (e.g., inability to reproduce ExPLORe's original hyperparameters) and limitations section that is candid about architecture, generalization, and real-world applicability gaps.
weaknesses: The theoretical analysis in Appendix B is weak and relies on strong, unjustified/hand-wavy assumptions (e.g., a clean epsilon-separable partition between retrieved and non-retrieved offline data, an assumed monotonic relationship between the regularization coefficient and retrieval fraction, and a borrowed TRPO-style performance-difference bound); it reads more as post-hoc justification than rigorous theory and adds limited credibility to the empirical claims.

The two core techniques are largely recombinations of existing ideas: retrieval-augmented replay resembles prior offline-data-reuse methods (RLPD-style rehearsal with retrieval), and execution guidance is essentially a variant of JSRL with different behavior-cloning data and mid-episode switching; the novelty is incremental engineering rather than a fundamentally new algorithmic contribution.

Experiments use only 3 random seeds per task, which is a relatively small sample size for RL given typically high variance, especially considering the wide confidence intervals shown in several figures (e.g., Fig. 3, Fig. 6).
Comparisons claiming GSA at 150k samples 'matches' baseline performance at 500k-1M samples are somewhat qualitative/visual rather than backed by rigorous statistical testing.

The 'non-curated' offline datasets are still constructed in a fairly controlled manner (pretrained/noised policy rollouts for Meta-World, curiosity-driven unsupervised RL agents for DMControl) rather than being truly in-the-wild/internet-scale data, which may limit how well the claimed generality extends beyond the paper's specific data-generation pipeline.

Baseline reproduction issues are acknowledged (e.g., ExPLORe required substantial modification to get reasonable results), raising some concern about whether baseline comparisons are fully fair or optimally tuned.
Evaluation is entirely in simulation; no real-robot validation is provided despite claims about robotic manipulation relevance.
Minor clarity issues remain, such as inconsistent labeling in figures (e.g., Figure 1's task icons) and a typo referring to 'JSRL-BS' in the text, which slightly detract from polish.

strengths: Very extensive empirical evaluation spanning 72 visuomotor tasks across 6 embodiments (DMControl + Meta-World), which is substantially broader than prior world-model pretraining papers that typically test on a handful of tasks.

Clear, well-motivated problem diagnosis: the paper carefully identifies distributional shift between offline pretraining data and online fine-tuning data as the reason naive world-model fine-tuning fails, supported by a t-SNE/Wasserstein-distance analysis (Fig. 2).

Reasonably thorough ablation studies isolating the contribution of world-model pretraining, experience rehearsal, and execution guidance (Fig. 6, Fig. 11), as well as comparisons of fine-tuning different world-model sub-components (Fig. 8).

Comparisons against a wide range of relevant baselines (R3M, UDS, ExPLORe, JSRL-BC, iVideoGPT, PackNet, Diffusion Policy, DrQv2, DreamerV3), and an additional continual-learning experiment showing versatility of the approach.

Reasonable engineering novelty in combining retrieval-based rehearsal with a mid-episode behavior-cloning guidance schedule tailored to reward-free, multi-embodiment, non-expert data, differentiating it from RLPD/ExPLORe/JSRL which assume reward-labeled or task-specific data.
weaknesses: The theoretical analysis in Appendix B is weak and largely circular: Proposition 1's proof simply assumes by construction that retrieved samples have distance < ε and non-retrieved samples ≥ ε, which trivially yields the claimed inequality rather than proving anything substantive about the retrieval mechanism; Proposition 3 is essentially a restatement of the TRPO performance-difference lemma under a strong, unverified assumption (constant lower bound δ on advantage), offering little additional insight specific to this method.

The core claim of 'matching baseline performance with far fewer samples' is not fully supported by the paper's own tables: on Meta-World, GSA at 150k samples (mean 0.750) does not match DreamerV3 or DrQv2 at 1M samples (means 0.900/0.753), which is a fairly direct contradiction of the abstract/intro claims about matching 1M-sample performance with 150k samples.

The 'non-curated' offline dataset for Meta-World is constructed by rolling out pretrained TD-MPC2 expert policies (trained on the actual 50 tasks) with injected Gaussian noise; this is not truly reward-free, task-agnostic data in the way the framing suggests, since task-specific expert policies were used to generate it, which weakens the paper's central premise of leveraging genuinely uncurated, in-the-wild-like data.

The retrieval mechanism used for experience rehearsal depends on the encoder learned during world-model pretraining to measure neural feature similarity, but the paper does not analyze potential circularity/failure modes when this encoder itself is imperfect for novel or hard-exploration tasks, which are exactly the tasks the paper emphasizes as most challenging.

Baseline tuning appears asymmetric: the paper explicitly states they were unable to reproduce satisfactory ExPLORe performance with default hyperparameters and had to substantially modify its implementation (replacing RND with ensembles, sharing latent space), raising concerns about fairness of the comparison relative to the effort invested in tuning GSA.

All experiments are conducted purely in simulation (DMControl, Meta-World); despite strong motivating claims about robotics and multi-embodiment applicability, there is no real-robot validation, and the stated future work item to test in the real world undercuts the practical significance claims made in the introduction.

Only 3 random seeds are used per task across 72 tasks with substantial reported variance in some learning curves (e.g., Stick Pull, Assembly), which may be insufficient to support strong claims of consistent large margins over baselines, especially given RL's well-known seed sensitivity.

The method is largely a combination of existing ideas (RLPD/ExPLORe-style offline data replay, JSRL-style behavior-cloning guidance, nearest-neighbor retrieval) adapted to a world-model setting, and the individual novelty of each component is somewhat incremental relative to the cited prior work.

strengths: Addresses a realistic and underexplored problem setting: leveraging reward-free, mixed-quality, multi-embodiment offline data for RL, which lifts several restrictive assumptions made by prior offline-to-online RL work.

Very extensive empirical evaluation spanning 72 visuomotor tasks across DMControl and Meta-World (locomotion and manipulation), roughly 12x more tasks than prior world-model pretraining baselines, which substantially strengthens the credibility of the claims.

Clear diagnosis of the failure mode (distributional shift between offline pretraining data and online fine-tuning data) supported by qualitative (t-SNE) and quantitative (Wasserstein distance) evidence in Fig. 2.
The two proposed techniques (experience rehearsal via retrieval, and execution guidance via a scheduled BC prior policy) are simple, well-motivated, and directly target the identified failure mode.

Strong empirical results: large relative improvement (102.8%) over learning-from-scratch baselines, and clear outperformance of multiple recent baselines that leverage offline data (R3M, UDS, ExPLORe, JSRL-BC) as well as SOTA world-model pretraining methods (iVideoGPT, pretrained DreamerV3) without relying on reward shaping or expert replay buffer initialization.

Thorough ablations isolating the contribution of pretraining, experience rehearsal, and execution guidance (Fig. 6-8), plus comparison against an alternative uncertainty-based reward-labeling strategy (OTS/ExPLORe-style), which helps justify design choices.
Additional continual-learning experiment (Ant task sequence) demonstrates a further practical benefit of the approach beyond the main setting.
Good reproducibility effort: detailed algorithm box, hyperparameters, network architectures, and compute resource reporting in the appendix.
weaknesses: The theoretical analysis in Appendix B is fairly superficial: Proposition 1 essentially assumes the desired inequality via the retrieval construction (data selected to be within epsilon of online distribution) rather than deriving it from first principles, and Proposition 3 relies on directly importing the TRPO performance-difference lemma with strong, largely unverifiable assumptions (guide policy uniformly better by a fixed margin), limiting its explanatory value beyond providing intuition.

The architectural contribution is minimal (a fairly standard RSSM with zero-padded actions and removed task losses); the paper's main contribution is the fine-tuning recipe rather than a fundamentally new modeling approach, which the authors acknowledge.

Baseline reproduction concerns: the authors explicitly note difficulty reproducing satisfactory ExPLORe performance with the original codebase/hyperparameters and had to substantially modify the method (replacing RND with ensembles, sharing latent space), which raises questions about whether the baseline comparison is fully fair/optimized.

The Meta-World portion of the 'non-curated' dataset is constructed by adding Gaussian noise to trajectories from pretrained expert RL agents (TDMPC v2), which is a fairly controlled/synthetic way of producing 'mixed quality' data and may not fully capture the diversity/messiness of truly in-the-wild, non-curated datasets.
All experiments are conducted purely in simulation; no real-robot validation is provided, despite motivating the method with real-world data-collection costs.

Some individual task curves (e.g., Fig. 3 right, Fig. 6) show quite large confidence intervals, and no aggregate statistical significance test (e.g., across seeds/tasks) is reported beyond visual CIs and IQM/optimality-gap plots in the appendix.

The retrieval-based experience rehearsal assumes offline data spans the same task/embodiment family as the downstream task (in-domain data), so generalization to substantially different embodiments or domains remains unclear, as acknowledged in the limitations.

strengths: Very extensive empirical evaluation across 72 visuomotor tasks spanning 6 embodiments (DMControl locomotion and Meta-World manipulation), which is substantially broader than prior world-model-pretraining works that were evaluated on a handful of tasks.

Clear and well-motivated diagnosis of the failure mode of naive world-model fine-tuning (distributional shift between offline pretraining data and online fine-tuning data), supported by t-SNE visualizations and Wasserstein distance measurements.

The two proposed techniques (retrieval-based experience rehearsal and execution guidance via a mixed BC/RL policy) are simple, computationally cheap (Faiss-based retrieval in seconds), and shown to meaningfully improve performance through careful ablations.

Thorough set of ablation studies: component-wise ablation (P/ER/G), hyperparameter sensitivity for the guidance schedule, robustness to degraded retrieval quality, world-model component fine-tuning analysis, and model-size-matched comparisons with DreamerV3.

Comparisons against a wide and relevant set of baselines (R3M, UDS-RLPD, ExPLORe, JSRL-BC, DrQ-v2, DreamerV3, iVideoGPT, PackNet), including an aligned re-implementation of iVideoGPT to remove confounds like reward shaping and buffer pre-filling.
Good reproducibility support: detailed hyperparameters, full algorithm box, compute resource reporting, and disclosed baseline implementation choices/limitations.
Additional continual-learning experiment showing the pretrained world model and reuse mechanisms generalize beyond the single-task fine-tuning setting.
weaknesses: The theoretical analysis (Propositions 1 and 2) is fairly informal and somewhat tautological (e.g., Proposition 1's proof essentially assumes the desired inequality via an artificial threshold-based partition of the offline data), so it provides limited rigorous justification beyond the empirical demonstration.

The Meta-World "non-curated" dataset is synthetically constructed by injecting Gaussian noise into a trained TD-MPC2 expert policy, which is a stylized proxy for genuinely non-curated data (e.g., crowd-sourced, in-the-wild, or multi-source teleoperation data) and may not fully capture the heterogeneity and embodiment/action-space mismatches present in real non-curated datasets.

Experience rehearsal fundamentally relies on the offline dataset containing trajectories relevant to the downstream task (via nearest-neighbor retrieval in encoder feature space); if the non-curated data has poor coverage of the target task (as could easily occur with truly diverse, task-agnostic data), the method's benefits are less clear, and this dependency is not deeply analyzed beyond one precision table on 4 tasks.

Some baseline comparisons rely on modified/re-tuned implementations (e.g., ExPLORe required replacing RND with ensembles and other changes because the original hyperparameters failed), which, while transparently disclosed, raises questions about whether comparisons are fully fair to competing methods.

Performance is not uniformly superior: several tasks show NCRL underperforming baselines at larger sample budgets (e.g., Pick Place, Reach, Peg Unplug Side, Acrobot Swingup Hard), and some tasks (Disassemble) fail entirely for all methods, without deeper discussion of when/why the approach may not help.
The core world-model architecture (RSSM/DreamerV3-style) is not novel; the contribution is primarily in the fine-tuning pipeline, which is acknowledged but limits the technical novelty of the paper.
Evaluation is restricted to simulated benchmarks; no real-robot validation, and the paper's own limitations section admits generalization to new embodiments/configurations remains challenging.

strengths: The paper tackles a well-motivated and practically relevant problem: leveraging non-curated, reward-free, mixed-quality, multi-embodiment offline data for sample-efficient RL, which is more realistic than assuming curated reward-labeled offline data.

Extensive empirical evaluation across 72 tasks spanning DMControl and Meta-World, which is broader than prior world-model pretraining papers (e.g., iVideoGPT, Seo et al.) that were evaluated on a handful of tasks.

The two proposed components (experience rehearsal via retrieval, and execution guidance via a mixed prior/RL policy schedule) are simple, computationally lightweight (Faiss-based retrieval), and are ablated individually, showing incremental contributions.

Reasonably thorough set of baselines (R3M, UDS-RLPD, ExPLORe, JSRL-BC, DreamerV3, DrQ-v2, iVideoGPT, PackNet) and several supplementary analyses (retrieval precision, robustness to retrieval corruption, hyperparameter sensitivity, model-size-matched comparisons).
Attempt at theoretical justification for the two proposed techniques (Propositions 1 and 2), tying method design to intuitive principles of distribution shift and policy improvement bounds.
weaknesses: The theoretical results are weak and somewhat vacuous: Proposition 1's proof simply assumes by construction that retrieved data is closer to online data than the rest of the offline data (via an artificial epsilon threshold), which is close to tautological rather than a meaningful guarantee; Proposition 2 is essentially a direct restatement of Kakade & Langford's conservative policy iteration bound with symbols relabeled, and the claimed 'improvement' condition depends on an unverifiable advantage term and an error bound epsilon that is not empirically estimated or connected back to real quantities in the experiments.

The dataset used for Meta-World is synthetically constructed by injecting Gaussian noise into TD-MPC2 expert policies to simulate 'mixed-quality' data, and the DMControl offline data comes from unsupervised RL agents already trained specifically to be exploratory. This is a fairly favorable, self-generated data setup rather than genuinely 'in-the-wild' non-curated data (e.g., human teleoperation, YouTube videos, or cross-task/cross-domain corpora), which somewhat undercuts the paper's core motivating claim of using 'abundant non-curated data' realistically -- the offline data is still in-domain and algorithmically curated to have useful coverage.

Comparisons to prior offline-to-online baselines (RLPD, ExPLORe, UDS) are handicapped by giving those baselines only 'task-relevant' pre-filtered offline data while NCRL gets to use its retrieval mechanism on the full non-curated pool; combined with the paper's own admission that they could not reproduce good ExPLORe results and had to substantially modify it (replacing RND with ensembles, sharing latent space), this raises concerns about baseline tuning parity and fairness of comparison.

Some experimental results are internally inconsistent or concerning: e.g., DreamerV3 with the same larger model size sometimes performs worse than the smaller model (Fig. 15), several MetaWorld tasks show quite low absolute success rates for NCRL at 150k steps (e.g., Pick Place 0.20, Disassemble 0.0, Soccer 0.16), and performance on some tasks is not dramatically better than baselines, undermining the 'nearly twice the aggregate score' headline claim as a general characterization.

The pretraining stage uses a very large 280M-parameter world model and reportedly ~48 GPU-hours per domain plus ~8 GPU-hours per 150k-step fine-tuning run (1728 GPU-hours to reproduce Fig. 3 results), which is a substantial computational overhead relative to the 150k-sample budget headline efficiency claim; the true cost-normalized comparison against baselines is not clearly presented.

The architectural contribution is minimal (essentially RSSM/DreamerV3 with zero-padded actions and removed task losses), and the two 'novel' techniques (nearest-neighbor retrieval-based replay, and behavior-cloning-based policy mixing/JSRL variant) are incremental combinations of existing ideas (RLPD/ExPLORe-style replay, JSRL) rather than fundamentally new mechanisms, despite the paper's claims of significant novelty.

The comparison in Fig. 4/iVideoGPT section is somewhat unfair as acknowledged by the authors themselves (different pretraining domains, no reward shaping/demo pre-filling for NCRL vs. baselines using these), and even in the 'aligned' setting (Fig. 10) improvements are inconsistent, e.g., large overlapping confidence intervals on several tasks.

Limited discussion of why performance is poor on specific hard tasks (Disassemble consistently 0.0 across all methods, low performance on Pick Place, Soccer) is relegated to appendix without much analysis, weakening the claim of broad and consistent applicability across the 72 tasks.

strengths: Extensive empirical evaluation across 72 diverse tasks spanning 6 embodiments (DMControl locomotion + Meta-World manipulation), substantially larger in scope than prior world-model pretraining works (e.g., Seo et al. 2022, Wu et al. 2024/2025) which were evaluated on only a handful of tasks.

Addresses a practically important and realistic problem setting: reward-free, mixed-quality, cross-embodiment offline data, which lowers the barrier for using offline data compared to standard offline RL settings that require curated, reward-labeled data.

Clear and convincing diagnosis of the core failure mode (distributional shift between pretraining and fine-tuning data) supported by both qualitative (t-SNE) and quantitative (Wasserstein distance) evidence in Fig. 2.

The two proposed techniques (experience rehearsal via retrieval, execution guidance via mixed BC/RL policy rollout) are simple, well-motivated, and supported by both ablations and theoretical arguments (Propositions 1 and 2, building on Kakade & Langford 2002).

Thorough ablation studies: component-wise contribution (Fig. 6/13), robustness to retrieval quality degradation (Fig. 14), sensitivity to execution-guidance schedule (Fig. 12), fair comparison across DreamerV3 model sizes (Fig. 15), and retrieval precision analysis (Table 2).

Strong comparison baseline coverage: R3M, UDS-RLPD, ExPLORe, JSRL-BC, Diffusion Policy, iVideoGPT, DreamerV3, DrQ-v2, and PackNet for continual learning, with an aligned re-implementation of iVideoGPT to control for confounding factors (reward shaping, demo pre-filling).
Good reproducibility: detailed algorithm box, hyperparameters, compute resource reporting, and disclosure of LLM usage.
weaknesses: The theoretical analysis (Appendix B) is more heuristic than rigorous: Proposition 1's proof relies on an unjustified epsilon-threshold construction of the retrieved subset, and the 'catastrophic forgetting' argument is an informal explanation rather than a formal guarantee.
The core architecture (RSSM/DreamerV3-style world model) is not novel; the main contribution is procedural (retrieval + guided rollout schedule) rather than an architectural or algorithmic advance.

Despite being termed 'non-curated,' the pretraining data is still generated by task-agnostic but purpose-built agents (unsupervised RL agents for DMControl, noise-injected TD-MPC2 experts for Meta-World) rather than truly in-the-wild/uncontrolled data as suggested in the framing; this is a narrower notion of 'non-curated' than the introduction implies.

Retrieval precision degrades for some tasks (e.g., 68% precision@500 for Door Open), and the method's reliance on a simple L2 distance in encoder feature space may not scale robustly to much larger or more diverse non-curated datasets than tested here.

Some individual-task results are weak or inconsistent (e.g., Disassemble 0.0 across all methods, Pick Place only 0.20 for NCRL vs. 0.67 for baselines at 1M steps, Peg Unplug Side slightly below baselines), which is only partially discussed.

Baseline reproduction required nontrivial modification (e.g., ExPLORe's RND replaced with ensembles due to failure to reproduce reported performance), raising some concern about comparison fairness even though the authors are transparent about this.
All evaluation is in simulation; no real-robot validation, which limits claims about practical applicability despite the robotics motivation.
